title: 1 Samuel 16:14–23
context: The Spirit of the LORD departs from Saul, and an evil spirit from the LORD troubles him. His servants suggest finding a skilled harpist, and one of them recommends a son of Jesse: skilled, brave, prudent in speech, handsome, and with the LORD’s presence. David comes to Saul’s court, wins his love, and becomes his armor bearer. Whenever the troubling spirit comes, David plays the harp and Saul is relieved. The scene brings the newly anointed David into the household of the king he will one day replace.

verses.text: Now the LORD’s Spirit departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the LORD troubled him.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s Spirit departs from Saul, and an evil spirit from the LORD troubles him. Arminian readers generally read the departure as the withdrawal of the empowering for kingship that had come on Saul (10:10).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the evil spirit as under God’s sovereign control, as in Judges 9:23; see the contrast noted there. Shared ground: both traditions read the Spirit’s departure here chiefly in terms of Saul’s office, and Psalm 51:11 may echo it.

verses.text: Saul’s servants said to him, “See now, an evil spirit from God troubles you.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul’s servants recognize that an evil spirit from God troubles him. Arminian readers note that the servants understand the affliction in religious terms, seeing God’s hand in Saul’s distress.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see even the servants acknowledging God’s rule over what is happening to the king. Both traditions read the verse as describing Saul’s condition in the language of the text, without claiming to know its exact nature.

verses.text: Let our lord now command your servants who are in front of you to seek out a man who is a skillful player on the harp. Then when the evil spirit from God is on you, he will play with his hand, and you will be well.”
verses.arminianNotes: The servants suggest finding a skilled harpist to play when the spirit comes. Arminian readers note the practical care of Saul’s servants, who seek a way to relieve their king’s suffering through music.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the suggestion God’s providence arranging the means to bring David into Saul’s court. Shared ground: music is offered as a remedy, and both traditions read the plan as a natural step that serves a larger purpose.

verses.text: Saul said to his servants, “Provide me now a man who can play well, and bring him to me.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul tells his servants to provide a skilled player. Arminian readers note that Saul accepts the advice readily, suggesting how severe his distress has become and how eager he is for relief.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Saul unknowingly inviting the man God has chosen to replace him. Both traditions read the verse as an ordinary command that the narrative uses to bring the anointed king and the rejected king together.

verses.text: Then one of the young men answered and said, “Behold, I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite who is skillful in playing, a mighty man of valor, a man of war, prudent in speech, and a handsome person; and the LORD is with him.”
verses.arminianNotes: A young man describes David: skilled, brave, a man of war, prudent in speech, handsome, and the LORD is with him. Arminian readers note the many qualities listed, crowned by God’s presence as the most important.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see “the LORD is with him” as the key phrase, contrasting with the Spirit’s departure from Saul. Shared ground: the description introduces David to the court and highlights God’s presence as the decisive mark of his life.

verses.text: Therefore Saul sent messengers to Jesse, and said, “Send me David your son, who is with the sheep.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul sends to Jesse for David, who is with the sheep. Arminian readers note the irony that Saul summons David from the same sheep where Samuel found him, without knowing about his anointing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s providence moving David from the fields to the palace through Saul’s own request. Both traditions read the verse as the next step in a story where human decisions serve the purposes God has already revealed.

verses.text: Jesse took a donkey loaded with bread, a container of wine, and a young goat, and sent them by David his son to Saul.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesse sends David with a donkey loaded with bread, wine, and a young goat. Arminian readers note the customary gift, a gesture of respect from a family sending a son to serve in the king’s household.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the gift as part of the ordinary courtesies through which David enters Saul’s service. Shared ground: the detail is practical, and both traditions read it as showing the proper respect owed to the king.

verses.text: David came to Saul and stood before him. He loved him greatly; and he became his armor bearer.
verses.arminianNotes: David comes to Saul, who loves him greatly and makes him his armor bearer. Arminian readers note the warmth of the first meeting, which makes Saul’s later jealousy (18:8–9) all the more tragic.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David placed close to Saul, learning the ways of the court under God’s direction. Both traditions read the verse as the high point of the relationship between the two men, before it turns to rivalry.

verses.text: Saul sent to Jesse, saying, “Please let David stand before me, for he has found favor in my sight.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul asks Jesse to let David stay, for he has found favor. Arminian readers note that David’s character and skill win Saul’s goodwill, showing the qualities that will mark his later leadership.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the favor David finds as a sign of God’s blessing on him. Shared ground: the request establishes David’s ongoing place at court, and both traditions read it as part of God’s preparation for David’s future role.

verses.text: When the spirit from God was on Saul, David took the harp and played with his hand; so Saul was refreshed and was well, and the evil spirit departed from him.
verses.arminianNotes: When the spirit troubles Saul, David plays the harp, and Saul is refreshed as the evil spirit departs. Arminian readers note the relief that comes through David’s music, showing his service to the king who will later turn on him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God using David’s skill as a means of mercy to Saul, even under judgment. Both traditions read the closing verse as a picture of David serving faithfully, and of temporary relief rather than a full restoration of Saul.
